Pour faciliter la création, [t0mg] a développé eenkY, un environnement de développement intégré (IDE) open source sous licence MIT, disponible sur GitHub. Ce logiciel permet de concevoir des livres dont vous êtes le héros ou des jeux d'aventure textuels, puis de les exécuter directement sur les liseuses Xteink. Une vidéo de démonstration illustre le fonctionnement du projet.

Les liseuses Xteink, souvent utilisées pour la lecture, se révèlent ainsi adaptées à des usages ludiques ou éducatifs. Leur compatibilité avec des firmwares personnalisés en fait des outils polyvalents, bien que certaines versions distribuées par des revendeurs tiers soient verrouillées, nécessitant un déverrouillage pour installer des logiciels tiers.
articles.body_en:
The eeink project, created by [t0mg], repurposes Xteink e-ink readers into platforms for interactive text adventures. These devices, powered by an ESP32 microcontroller, are popular for their compact size and affordability while remaining highly customizable. The X4 Pro model features an ESP32-S3 with additional RAM, while the X3/X4 versions use an ESP32-C3, which has stricter memory limitations.

The project focuses on adventures written in the ink scripting language, designed for interactive storytelling. To streamline development, [t0mg] created eenkY, an open-source integrated development environment (IDE) under the MIT license, available on GitHub. This tool enables users to design choose-your-own-adventure books or text-based games and run them directly on Xteink readers. A demo video demonstrates the project in action.

Originally intended for reading, Xteink devices prove versatile for gaming or educational purposes. Their support for custom firmware makes them adaptable, though some versions sold by third-party retailers are locked, requiring unlocking to install alternative software.

articles.t: WeatherPaper: a smart weather station using an e-paper display
articles.title_fr: WeatherPaper : une station météo connectée sur écran e-paper 4,2"
articles.title_en: WeatherPaper: A Smart Weather Station with a 4.2" E-Paper Display
articles.lead_fr: Une station météo autonome sur écran e-paper 4,2" avec plus d’un an d’autonomie et un montage mural discret.
articles.lead_en: A 4.2-inch e-paper weather station with over a year of battery life and a flush wall mount design.
articles.body_fr:
WeatherPaper se distingue par son écran e-paper de 4,2 pouces, intégré à une carte électronique conçue sur mesure. Son principal atout réside dans son autonomie exceptionnelle, dépassant 18 mois grâce à une gestion logicielle optimisée et un microcontrôleur sous-fréquencé. La connexion WiFi, bien que présente, est sollicitée de manière minimale pour préserver la batterie, avec des temps de récupération des données réduits à quelques millisecondes.

La configuration du réseau WiFi s’effectue sans effort via un portail captif (captive portal), évitant ainsi la saisie manuelle des identifiants ou des clés d’API dans le code. L’appareil propose également un montage mural discret grâce à un système de fixation intégré à son boîtier en résine givrée, qui met en valeur les composants internes plutôt que de les dissimuler.

Entièrement open-source, WeatherPaper permet aux utilisateurs de modifier l’affichage des données météorologiques selon leurs besoins. Les plans détaillés du projet sont disponibles sur Instructables, tandis que le code source est hébergé sur GitHub pour une personnalisation avancée.
articles.body_en:
WeatherPaper features a 4.2-inch e-paper display paired with a custom PCB, designed for long-term use. Its standout feature is its battery life, exceeding 18 months thanks to aggressive power management, including software optimizations and underclocking the microcontroller. WiFi connectivity is used sparingly, with data fetching times reduced to milliseconds to minimize power consumption.

The device simplifies WiFi setup using a captive portal, eliminating the need to hardcode network credentials or API keys into the firmware. Its design includes a frosted resin enclosure that highlights internal components rather than hiding them, and a built-in screw mount for a flush wall installation.

WeatherPaper is fully open-source, allowing users to customize the weather data displayed. Detailed project instructions are available on Instructables, while the source code is hosted on GitHub for further modifications.

articles.t: M5Stack Paper Mono – An ESP32-S3 e-paper development board with 3.97-inch touchscreen, LoRa, and NFC
articles.title_fr: M5Stack Paper Mono : carte de développement e-paper ESP32-S3 avec écran tactile et connectivité LoRa/NFC
articles.title_en: M5Stack Paper Mono: ESP32-S3 E-Paper Dev Board with 3.97-inch Touchscreen, LoRa, and NFC
articles.lead_fr: M5Stack lance une nouvelle carte de développement e-paper basée sur l'ESP32-S3, dotée d'un écran tactile 3,97" monochrome, de LoRa et NFC.
articles.lead_en: M5Stack has launched a new ESP32-S3-based e-paper development board featuring a 3.97-inch monochrome touchscreen, LoRa, and NFC connectivity.
articles.body_fr:
M5Stack enrichit sa gamme de cartes de développement dédiées aux écrans e-paper avec le Paper Mono, une solution basée sur le microcontrôleur ESP32-S3R8 d’Espressif. Ce modèle se distingue par un écran tactile monochrome de 3,97 pouces, offrant des taux de rafraîchissement plus rapides que son prédécesseur, le PaperColor.

La carte intègre plusieurs composants pour des applications variées : 8 Mo de PSRAM et 16 Mo de mémoire flash, un slot pour carte microSD, ainsi qu’un microphone PDM et un buzzer pour des interactions audio. Un capteur IMU 6 axes (pour détecter les mouvements), un RTC (horloge en temps réel) et des boutons physiques complètent l’ensemble. Une LED RGB permet d’ajouter des indicateurs visuels. Côté connectivité, le Paper Mono propose le Wi-Fi 4 (2,4 GHz), le Bluetooth 5.0 LE (y compris Mesh), ainsi que les technologies LoRa et NFC pour des communications longue et courte portée.

Alimenté via un port USB-C et une batterie de 1 150 mAh, le Paper Mono est disponible en deux versions : une standard incluant LoRa et NFC, et une Lite dépourvue de ces modules. Aucune option d’extension n’est prévue sur cette carte.
articles.body_en:
M5Stack has expanded its e-paper development board lineup with the Paper Mono, a new ESP32-S3-based board featuring a 3.97-inch monochrome touchscreen display. Designed for faster refresh rates than its predecessor, the PaperColor, this kit targets projects requiring responsive e-paper interfaces.

The board includes 8MB of PSRAM, 16MB of flash storage, a microSD card slot, and audio capabilities with a PDM microphone and buzzer. Additional features include a 6-axis IMU for motion tracking, an RTC for timekeeping, and physical buttons alongside an RGB LED for status indication. Connectivity options cover 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi 4, Bluetooth 5.0 LE (including Mesh), LoRa for long-range communication, and NFC for short-range interactions.

Powered through a USB-C port and a 1150 mAh battery, the Paper Mono is available in two variants: a standard version with LoRa and NFC, and a Lite version without these features. The board does not include any expansion ports.

articles.t: Track Bird Visitors With a Raspberry Pi and a USB Mic
articles.title_fr: Un Raspberry Pi et un micro pour suivre les oiseaux avec un écran e-ink
articles.title_en: Track Birds with Raspberry Pi, Mic, and E-Ink Display
articles.lead_fr: Un projet DIY utilise l’IA pour identifier les oiseaux par leur chant et affiche les résultats sur un écran e-ink.
articles.lead_en: A DIY project uses AI to identify birds by their songs and displays results on an e-ink screen.
articles.body_fr:
Le projet Avian Visitors, développé par Teddy Warner, combine un Raspberry Pi et un microphone USB pour détecter et classer les oiseaux visitant un jardin grâce à l’intelligence artificielle. L’outil repose sur BirdNET, un modèle de deep learning open source issu de Cornell, capable de reconnaître plus de 11 000 espèces à partir de leur chant. Le système génère ensuite une illustration colorée sur une interface web, où la taille des images des oiseaux reflète leur fréquence d’apparition.

Une fonctionnalité originale consiste en l’ajout d’un écran e-ink en couleur, optionnel, qui affiche un résumé des 24 dernières heures de détections sous forme de collage. Les données peuvent aussi être envoyées vers Home Assistant ou via MQTT pour automatiser des actions en fonction des espèces observées. Le projet inclut un dépôt GitHub complet et une vidéo de démonstration pour faciliter la reproduction.

Pour fonctionner, le dispositif nécessite uniquement un Raspberry Pi et un microphone USB. BirdNET, développé par l’université Cornell, est accessible gratuitement et permet une identification fiable des oiseaux par leur vocalisation. Le projet s’inscrit dans une démarche artistique, transformant les données en une œuvre murale dynamique.
articles.body_en:
The Avian Visitors project by Teddy Warner uses a Raspberry Pi and a USB microphone to track and identify birds visiting a garden using artificial intelligence. The system relies on BirdNET, an open-source deep learning model from Cornell University, which can recognize over 11,000 bird species based solely on their songs. It then generates a colorful illustration on a web interface, where the size of each bird’s image reflects its detection frequency.

A standout feature is the optional color e-ink display, which shows a 24-hour summary of detected birds in a collage format. The data can also be sent to Home Assistant or via MQTT to trigger automations based on specific bird species. The project includes a full GitHub repository and a build video to guide users through the setup.

The setup requires only a Raspberry Pi and a USB microphone. BirdNET, developed by Cornell University, is freely available and provides reliable bird identification through vocalizations. The project blends technology and art, turning raw data into an evolving mural.

articles.t: ZecTrix Note 4 – A 4.2-inch ESP32-S3 wireless e-paper display for voice tasks
articles.title_fr: ZecTrix Note 4 : un écran e-ink ESP32-S3 avec reconnaissance vocale
articles.title_en: ZecTrix Note 4: ESP32-S3 E-Ink Display with Voice Recognition
articles.lead_fr: Un écran e-ink ESP32-S3 de 4,2 pouces intègre reconnaissance vocale, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth et NFC pour des notes intelligentes.
articles.lead_en: A 4.2-inch ESP32-S3 e-ink display with voice recognition, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and NFC for smart notes.
articles.body_fr:
Le ZecTrix Note 4, conçu par le laboratoire chinois ZecTrix Lab, est un écran e-ink intelligent basé sur un microcontrôleur ESP32-S3. Il se distingue par sa capacité à traiter des commandes vocales grâce à un microphone intégré et un haut-parleur. Son écran e-ink de 4,2 pouces affiche des rappels, des notes, des horloges, des informations météo, des images ou encore des modèles personnalisés. Une version alternative, le Note 4C, remplace l'écran monochrome par un panneau e-ink quatre couleurs (BWRY).

Le système embarqué repose sur un processeur ESP32-S3 d'Espressif Systems, doté de deux cœurs Tensilica LX7 cadencés jusqu'à 240 MHz et optimisés pour les tâches d'intelligence artificielle et d'apprentissage automatique. queue.rss: We’re living in 2026 and everyone knows that they can ask a large language model (LLM) a question and get an answer. But most people assume that requires an internet connection, because those LLMs live in massive data centers. The truth is that LLMs can run on local hardware, answering questions without any internet at all. Cameron Coward, of the Serial Hobbyism YouTube channel, took advantage of that fact, connecting an Arduino UNO Q to a vintage terminal . That terminal is a Texas Instruments Silent 700 (Model 745), which is a paper terminal that was made in the 1970s. Back then, it would have been used as an input/output device for something like a minicomputer, connected through either an acoustic coupler (remote) or RS232 (local). Users would type commands on the keyboard and computer output would print on the thermal paper. For this project, Coward connected the Silent 700 to his custom-built device, Termi3, to give it the ability to answer questions. The user types a question and a moment later, the terminal prints out the answer. As the name suggests, Termi3 is the third version of the device. The first two required internet access, because they retrieved answers through the Wolfram Alpha API. Termi3 doesn’t need any internet connection at all, because it generates an answer locally on an UNO Q (2GB) . The Arduino runs a local LLM, Llama 3.2-1B, on the Linux side without ever touching a network. It interfaces with the terminal though bit-banging on the STM32 side, which goes through a MAX3232 transceiver (for level conversion) to the terminal’s RS232 port. It is amazing that an LLM can run on the small and affordable UNO Q at all, especially with 2GB of RAM. So, the LLM isn’t particularly sophisticated and its answers aren’t always accurate — or even coherent. But they are often entertaining, which makes Termi3 a lot of fun to talk to. But it became a fan favorite and that in-universe model, the MSE-6, appears throughout subsequent movies, TV shows, and video games. All of them, however, are identical. Cass (the maker behind Chaos Theory) imagined how mouse droids would actually fit into the world and the result is this MSE-6 that knows how to party . According to the lore, billions of MSE-6 droids were built. For those living in the Star Wars universe, they wouldn’t be any more special than toasters or Huffy bicycles. It is only natural that individuals in that universe would customize mouse droids and Cass’ creation is an exploration of the kind of personalization that Sabine Wren would perform. For those who aren’t deep into Star Wars lore, the simpler explanation is that this is an adorable mouse droid capable of navigating autonomously and features blinky lights, a radical paint job, and a rave mode. In that mode, it turns into a graffiti-covered mobile party machine that spins around while blasting music and flashing its lights. Underneath the 3D-printed shell in that iconic shape, this is an Arduino UNO Rev3 -controlled rover robot. It has a pair of motors, which the Arduino controls through an L298N driver. Power comes from a 7.4V lithium battery pack, with a buck converter to reach 5V. An ultrasonic sensor prevents collisions and the sound plays through a DFPlayer Mini MP3 module. Finally, arrays of 5mm red LEDs provide visual flair. That all came together thanks to Cass’ fantastic paint job. She explains her inspiration, thought process, and supplies, but the great results are mostly attributable to her artistic talent. It is exactly the kind of mouse droid that Sabine Wren would adopt . queue.rss: Not since the seminal 1993 film Hocus Pocus has there been a more iconic book than Raspberry Pi Book of Making 2027 , and we thought it timely to share this project from its pages, which are packed with our favourite maker projects from the past year. You can get your copy at an introductory price of £9.99, but for now, let’s animate a Halloween skeleton with a $4 Raspberry Pi Pico . As October draws close, the veil between the worlds of the living and the dead grows thin, allowing spirits to cross. At least, that’s what watching too many horror/comedy films has taught us. Since the real world is rarely as interesting as Hollywood depicts, we’re not going to rely on the dead rising up, and give Halloween a helping hand by creating our own animated skeleton. You can build your own by following along, or adapt the techniques to animate whatever spooky (or not spooky) decorations you like. Our build starts with a 90cm glow-in-the-dark skeleton that we purchased from AliExpress. The key part of this build relies on it being a ‘2D’ skeleton where all the joints move in the same plane. There are some 3D skeletons available that are more anatomically accurate, but also harder to animate. Unfortunately, it can be a little hard to work out from the listing whether it’s a 2D or 3D skeleton, but if it’s 90cm, glow-in-the-dark, and about £3, then it should be the right one. The skeleton came as ten separate parts: two for each limb, one for the body, and one for the head. We’re going to add control to the hip and shoulder joints, meaning that our skeleton can perform a few moves. The knees and elbows we’ll leave loose to flail around. Before we get to all that though, we need a few additional parts. The skeleton is very flimsy, so we need a firm backing that we can place it on to keep everything in place. We used Oriented Strand Board (more commonly known as OSB) because we happened to have some available, but plywood would also work well. It needs to be at least 45 × 21cm, though if it’s bigger, that’s fine (and might protect your skeleton a bit more). We painted ours black to blend into the dark night. For the motion, we used servos. Servos are a little like motors in that you send a signal to make them turn, but unlike motors, they are used for turning a particular amount and usually operate a range of about 180 degrees. You send the servo a signal to let it know the angle you want, and it turns to that angle. There are — arguably — better ways to join four wires together and insulate the joint, but they all require more parts and complexity than a solder joint and self-amalgamating tape Servos come in different sizes and strengths, and we opted for 9g servos, which are just about strong enough for this. If you use anything bigger, you might find that they draw too much current, so we’d recommend sticking with little ones unless you want to add an external power supply. We wanted our skeleton to react to people around it, so we added a distance sensor to detect when someone is close to it. Finally, we need a controller to make everything do what we want it to. A Raspberry Pi computer will do the job, but for simplicity, we’ve used a Raspberry Pi Pico. Ours is a Raspberry Pi Pico W , but we’re not using the wireless interface, so any model should do just fine. Always make sure you position your servos before connecting the horns You’ll also need a few 3.5mm-wide screws that are smaller than your board is thick, some mounting hardware, and a cable tie. Bare bones Our skeleton came with moveable joints with a pin-and-socket connector. Our first thought was to keep these as hinges and then hook up an actuator to the limbs to pull them into the position we want (like making a puppet). However, we found that the flimsy plastic of the skeleton had a habit of twisting rather than rotating properly at the joint, so we needed a different plan. The first step is to disconnect the limbs from the skeleton — they should simply pop out. We’re not going to join our skeleton directly, but rather have the servos mounted to the limbs and held in place near the joint on the main body. Make sure Raspberry Pi Pico is mounted in such a way that you can access the USB port We now need a way of attaching a servo to each limb. Servos have a press-fit drive shaft that connects tightly to ‘horns’, and you usually get a selection of different-shaped horns with your servo. We used the single horn and screwed it close to the original joint. Your servos should come with screws that go through the holes on the horn. The only problem with these is that they poke through the thin plastic of the skeleton and could scratch someone who gets too close. You can use a blob of hot glue or attach a small bit of plastic or wood to the end of the screws if you’re worried about this. Power, ground, and data — three connections that let you add as many LEDs as you need Once you have the horns attached to each limb, you now need to worry about the other side of the servos. Servos do have mounting screws, but these are usually higher up the servo, designed for a recess, so we need some form of mount to hold them in place. If you have access to a 3D printer, then the easiest option is to print one. We used this one , but depending on your servo, you might need to use a different option. The important thing is that it holds the servo vertically. Your servos should come with mounting hardware Screw the horns onto the limbs as close as possible to the original joint If you don’t have access to a 3D printer, it should be possible to create a hole in your backing wood — either by chain-drilling or by drilling a starter hole and using a jigsaw — then mount the servo in there (perhaps with a liberal amount of hot glue). Once you have your servo mounts, you should have all the key pieces of your motion-control hardware. Eye lights It’s well established in cinema that scary things have red eyes. We’re not really sure why this is, since the only thing this author has ever seen with red eyes was an albino rabbit, and that little ball of fluff was the least scary thing in existence. However, since that is the established trope, our skeleton should have red eyes. Don’t tell your woodworking teacher, but wiggling the drill a little as you make the eye holes makes it easier to mount the LEDs There are a couple of options for this: we could use red LEDs, or we could use RGB LEDs and just neglect two of the three colours. Although the latter option might seem a bit wasteful, it simplifies the build a bit and gives us options for the future, so we’ll go with it. The specific LEDs we’ll use are 12mm WS2811 LEDs. These come in chains (usually of 50) running at either 5V or 12V. We want the 5V version, and we just need two of the LEDs, but we can cut these from a chain. queue.rss: A recent article revealed that OpenAI is purchasing tens of thousands of Mac minis and Mac Studios to give AI agents dedicated environments to run, make mistakes, and learn. It’s a smart infrastructure decision for agents meant to operate inside a computer clicking, navigating, using software: they need a full computer to practice on. But it got us wondering: is that always the right environment for an agent? Why agents need their own environment An AI agent isn’t a chatbot. It perceives a situation, takes an action, observes the result, adjusts, and tries again – in a loop that requires a persistent local environment with compute, I/O, and feedback. You can’t outsource the whole thing to a cloud API, because the agent needs somewhere to live and something to interact with. In OpenAI’s situation, the answer is: give it a computer. That works well when the goal is teaching agents to use software. But software isn’t the whole world. Physical AI needs something different (and surprisingly cheaper) A Mac mini today starts at around $900. At the scale OpenAI is reportedly operating, the infrastructure bill is substantial. That cost is justified when you need a full computing environment. But what if the agent’s environment doesn’t need to be a general-purpose computer? What if it needs to be a temperature sensor, a camera feed, a production line? At a fraction of the cost, an Arduino ® VENTUNO Q board can provide a persistent Linux environment for the agent runtime, local AI inference, and direct access to real-world I/O: cameras, sensors, actuators. The economics of deploying agent environments at scale look very different when each node costs significantly less, and can be embedded directly in the physical context it’s meant to ultimately operate in. What an Arduino agentic environment actually looks like VENTUNO Q is built to combine a Linux-capable MPU with NPU acceleration and a dedicated real-time MCU on a single board. The Linux side is engineered to run the agent – its reasoning, its model, its decision logic. The MCU side is designed to connect it to the world: motors, sensors, cameras, industrial interfaces. No cloud dependency. No separate controller. One self-contained unit that perceives, decides, and acts. Arduino ® UNO Q is structured to extend this further as a low-cost remote node. David Groom demonstrated this clearly leveraging OpenClaw , developing an agent framework on UNO Q designed to enable agents to interact with physical hardware. By connecting to Arduino shields and accessing additional hardware capabilities, the framework supports physical-world interactions while enabling deployment across multiple units simultaneously, each maintaining its own context and operational role. Read about David Groom’s OpenClaw project here . With these tools, it’s easy to envision a “swarm” model: VENTUNO Q built to serve as a local processing hub, with UNO Q units designed for distributed deployment as remote nodes , all supporting agent-based workflows that interact with physical environments rather than simulated ones. More agents, more learning, lower cost This is where the conversation becomes more interesting than individual compute specifications alone. Lower deployment costs can make broader deployment economically feasible, creating opportunities for more agent interactions, richer feedback loops, and exposure to a wider range of real-world operating conditions. An agent that has operated across multiple physical environments, each with its own sensors, lighting conditions, and sources of noise, may be exposed to a broader set of inputs than an agent trained exclusively in software simulations. Arduino can give agents something else to learn from: the physical world. By combining accessible hardware with scalable deployment models, Arduino platforms are designed to support the creation of large numbers of agent-enabled environments for experimentation, testing, and real-world interaction. Ready to build your own agentic environment? queue.rss: The latest issue of Raspberry Pi Official Magazine — out now — features this Raspberry Pi 3 – based underwater camera that investigates water quality and organisms. Unboxed STEM Club consists of three friends aged 10 to 13 who meet up each weekend, along with two enthusiastic dads. The boys’ defining approach is to ask lots of questions, “look at problems as connected puzzles with many possible answers”, and keep trying hands-on solutions even if things go wrong at first. The airtight tube houses a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ and a Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 on a custom 3D-printed base, plus a temperature sensor Pinak, Vihaan, and Yuvan, along with their mentors Kshitij Varma and Dr Amol Patil, were excited by the idea of tackling a hands-on science, engineering, and coding project. They were inspired by the fact that we often talk about protecting oceans and rivers, but rarely have the tools to measure what’s happening below the surface and in the depths. Raspberry Pi had huge appeal as a compact computer that they could write code for themselves, connect to a wide variety of sensors, and use to directly control a Camera Module. Although they hadn’t used Raspberry Pi for STEM Club projects before, they realised it was an obvious choice for their citizen science aims, particularly as it came with an impressive online resource: thousands of willing and helpful fellow Raspberry Pi users. The fact that the whole build would come in at around £130 and could largely be built by the boys, with minimal adult supervision, set it apart from most underwater explorers in terms of both complexity and cost. What lies beneath? Sensea was conceived as “a low-cost DIY underwater explorer that would reveal what’s going on below the surface of our local ponds and rivers”, proving that you don’t need expensive equipment to investigate the depths. For context, the boys’ agitated pleas for a GoPro fell on deaf ears, so they built a custom camera rig instead, based around Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ . Not only was this solution more affordable, but it also had the advantage of low power consumption, running off a standard 5V USB power pack for longer. The team hoped the project might catch the imagination of other hobbyist makers, so these were important practical considerations. The most important aspect of all was how to keep the electronics dry. The container needed to be completely waterproof at all times while still allowing the sensors to measure the surrounding water and the camera to see clearly. It also needed to be opened and resealed to insert delicate sensors and rechargeable batteries, which made for quite the engineering challenge. The team designed a sealed acrylic tube that acts as a transparent pressure chamber, keeping the electronics dry while allowing the camera to see through its end cap. One end is permanently sealed with a 10.5cm acrylic disc bonded using marine epoxy. A waterproof cable gland is drilled through this end, allowing the DS18B20 temperature probe cable to pass through while maintaining a watertight seal. At the other end is an expanding drain plug of the sort used by plumbers to check for leaks. Rather than using propellers, Sensea sinks to the river or lake bed using a 2kg dumbbell as ballast The setup proved reliable and, crucially, dependably waterproof. Nonetheless, Sensea’s makers implemented a leak test regime that sees the fully sealed Sensea tube and cable submerged in a bucket of water for five minutes, to check for rising bubbles. Once this critical test is complete, the tube is lowered into the water in its protective cage. Getting the buoyancy and descent right was another challenge. A 2kg bone-shaped dumbbell, selected after many experiments with size and weight, ensures the Sensea sinks beneath the river surface, ready to start recording what its Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 can see. Exploring the murky depths The Camera Module captures 10-second underwater video clips and logs time-stamped water temperature readings from a waterproof DS18B20 sensor. The team settled on a manual fixed focus, since autofocus was likely to struggle when encountering suspended particles in the river. “Fixing the focus gives much sharper and more stable footage,” they explain. Unboxed STEM Club : The club comprises three young makers, and their adult mentors, who enjoy coding, science, and engineering The setup also includes a PCF8523 real-time clock that records accurate time stamps even without an internet connection. Video capture is triggered via a Python script called sensea_logger.py , which also measures the water temperature and ensures everything is written to Raspberry Pi’s microSD card for post-submersion retrieval. For their initial deployments, the team compared temperature measurements from the River Cam and a nearby lake called Todd’s Pit, clearly revealing differences between the two environments. Future additions may include a pH sensor for pollution monitoring, a depth or pressure sensor, and even AI-powered species identification. A similar setup could be used to monitor air quality, greenhouse conditions, or surface water from a floating buoy. Since we met the boys, the project has gone on to win Instructables’ Sensors Contest. Congratulations on a richly deserved win. Issue 170 of Raspberry Pi Official Magazine is out NOW! queue.rss: Internet radios have been a thing in some form for the last quarter century, and the advent of cheap networked microcontrollers has made them easier than ever to build. But just how small can one be made? [Milen] has made one that’s about as small as we’ve seen, and put it up on Instructables . The hardware recipe is straightforward enough; take a microcontroller, connect it to the internet, and have your internet radio software squirt its output to a DAC. In this case the microcontroller is an ESP32-C£ on a very small dev board, and clipped to that is a custom PCB with a PCM5102A I2S DAC and an amplifier. The whole thing is tiny, small enough in fact that the two connectors are significant in size compared to it. Whether or not it’s a practical device for listening remains to be seen, but it’s certainly tiny. But the question is, could it be made smaller? Perhaps eschewing the connectors would be an easy win, and in return for a loss in quality the ESP has a built-in DAC that’s not intended for audio but can be used. If you have any bright ideas, we’d be interested to hear them. We’ve seen plenty of internet radios over the years, and for some reason this cassette-shaped one appeals to us.

That’s where we find [Andy], or should we say, [Uncle Andrew]. Last Christmas he decided to scratch build an electronic busy board for his nephew , and while it might not be a terribly complex piece of kit from a technical standpoint, it’s a fantastic multidisciplinary project in that it’s really equal parts hardware and software. While it would surely be possible to implement a gadget like this entirely in hardware, [Andy] took the modern hobbyist approach of offloading some of the task to a collection of carefully arranged ones and zeros. In the write-up, [Andy] goes over the decisions he made while designing and building the device. This ranges from the extra effort put in to keep the PCB down to two layers and the logic behind LED multiplexing. This extends right into the software aspect of the project, with a surprisingly deep explanation of how the code uses timers and interrupts to run the show as efficiently as possible, maximizing the run time of the PIC18F67K40 microcontroller on a trio of AAA batteries. It’s a fun read about a low-stakes project that’s made all the better by the personal touch. Just like the kids of makers and hardware hackers , [Andy]’s nephew is a lucky to have somebody like this in his life.

queue.rss: Brain-computer interfaces may sound like the kind of hardware that requires a university lab and a massive budget to build, but Carlos Lorenzo-Zúñiga Marí managed to build one for less than $350. His custom eight-channel EEG headset combines a purpose-built biopotential acquisition board, an ESP32, dry electrodes, motion sensing, and 3D-printed hardware into a system capable of measuring electrical signals from the brain. That is a difficult thing to do because EEG signals are typically only around 10 to 100 microvolts by the time they reach the scalp. Electrical noise from mains wiring, chargers, lights, and other electronics can easily overwhelm them, as can the much stronger electrical signals produced by muscles. Carlos designed the acquisition board around an ADS1299, an eight-channel, 24-bit ADC made for measuring biopotential signals such as EEG. The circuit measures differences between electrodes rather than voltages relative to ground, helping reject noise appearing on both inputs. An active bias-drive circuit connected through ear-clip electrodes further reduces common-mode interference. An ESP32 microcontroller shares the four-layer PCB with the analog front end, providing processing and Wi-Fi connectivity. Keeping its high-frequency digital and RF signals away from the extremely sensitive EEG circuitry required careful PCB layout, including a dedicated internal ground plane and separation between analog and digital sections. There is also a six-axis IMU for identifying movement that could corrupt EEG measurements. A lightweight decision tree model monitors its data and generates hardware interrupts when it recognizes head movement, allowing affected portions of the EEG stream to be flagged as motion artifacts. The headset is based partly on OpenBCI's open source headwear design, with electrodes positioned according to the International 10-20 system. Spring-loaded dry electrodes eliminate conductive gel while helping maintain pressure against the scalp and through hair. Medical touchproof connectors carry the signals to a custom breakout PCB, which then connects to the acquisition board. Carlos also built the software needed to make the hardware useful. With no suitable ADS1299 driver available, he wrote his own implementation using SPI, DMA, and double buffering. That lets samples move into memory without tying up the ESP32's CPU during continuous acquisition. For safety purposes, the headset runs from a LiPo battery instead of mains power, and a galvanic isolator provides additional protection while connected to development equipment. When debugging uncovered a problem where USB power back-fed the 3.3 V rail, Carlos avoided another PCB revision by making a USB adapter that disconnects the 5 V line while leaving the data lines intact. Testing the finished board with its ADC inputs shorted produced a noise floor around one microvolt, close to the ADS1299's expected performance. The system then successfully recorded EMG and ECG signals before moving on to EEG, where it captured recognizable alpha-wave activity. Carlos' DIY hardware isn't going to perform as well as pricey commercial solutions. But for the home hobbyist, his system is pretty hard to beat.Testing a DIY brain-computer interface (📷: Carlos Lorenzo-Zúñiga Marí) The headset and signal acquisition hardware (📷: Carlos Lorenzo-Zúñiga Marí)

queue.rss: Before a hardware wallet can protect your cryptocurrency, it needs a seed phrase. Most wallets generate that phrase automatically, leaving users to trust that the device produced truly random words and handled them securely. Seedmate focuses entirely on that first step. Rather than generating a seed behind the scenes, the handheld device lets users create, verify, and manipulate BIP39 seed phrases offline using randomness they can see and provide themselves. Seedmate is a dedicated, air-gapped BIP39 calculator. It never connects to a computer, smartphone, or the internet, and there is no USB data interface, wireless radio, or companion application. Once the power switch is turned off, the device retains nothing in memory, making it completely stateless. Instead of asking users to trust a random number generator, Seedmate accepts entropy from the physical world. Dice rolls, coin flips, playing cards, or even words selected by hand can all be converted into a valid 12- or 24-word BIP39 mnemonic. One particularly interesting mode allows users to randomly choose 24 words themselves, with the device modifying only the final word so the checksum is correct. The remaining words stay exactly as they were chosen, and every calculation is displayed for manual verification. Seedmate can combine multiple independently created mnemonics using XOR, allowing users to mix entropy from several different sources into a single standard BIP39 seed. It also supports deterministic BIP85 child seed generation, making it possible to derive separate wallet seeds from one master mnemonic without creating additional random backups. The device includes several backup and recovery features aimed at eliminating single points of failure. Shamir's Secret Sharing can split a seed into as many as nine mnemonic shares, requiring only a chosen subset to reconstruct the original. Since every share is itself a valid BIP39 mnemonic, an individual share reveals nothing about the complete secret while still appearing perfectly ordinary. Seedmate also provides several reversible obfuscation methods for disguising physical backups. Bit shifting, logical inversion, and word-offset transformations can all produce another valid mnemonic that does not correspond to the original wallet. A triple mnemonic mode goes a step further by transforming one 24-word seed into two valid 12-word mnemonics that can be stored separately while also serving as convincing decoys. The hardware consists of a custom PCB built around a PIC32 microcontroller that runs firmware written entirely in C. User interaction comes through a keypad and a 128×160 color TFT display, while power is supplied by AAA batteries for more than 15 hours of operation. QR code export supports interoperability with projects such as Krux and SeedSigner, and an SD card can also be used for exporting data. At $55 , Seedmate occupies an unusual niche. It doesn't replace a hardware wallet or attempt to become one. Instead, it focuses entirely on the stage that many wallets treat as a one-time task: creating, splitting, combining, and protecting the seed phrase. For users who want every step of that process to be visible, repeatable, and verifiable offline, Seedmate fits the bill perfectly.A rendering of the device (📷: Seedmate) The hardware is very minimal (📷: Seedmate) The display board (📷: Seedmate)

queue.rss: Depth cameras are useful for everything from robots and navigation systems to computer vision projects, but they are typically pretty expensive. For this reason, they are not often used in hobbyist projects. But there is another approach, as was recently demonstrated by Depth Multitool. This device uses an ordinary USB webcam and an AI model running on the Arduino VENTUNO Q to estimate the distance to everything in view at 20 frames per second. There is no stereo camera, infrared projector, or LiDAR sensor involved. Created by Samuel Alexander, the project runs Depth Anything V2 Small directly on the VENTUNO Q's Qualcomm Dragonwing NPU. The 25-million-parameter neural network performs monocular depth estimation, meaning it looks at a single conventional camera image and predicts the relative distance of every pixel. The result is essentially a depth camera, only it is built almost entirely in software. Alexander turned that depth information into four interactive tools. Heatmap provides the most familiar view, blending the webcam image with a depth map where nearby objects appear bright and distant surfaces appear dark. Slicer is more interesting, highlighting only objects that fall within a selected depth range. The arrow keys move that range forward and backward or adjust its thickness, producing something resembling a movable cross-section of the room. Flood mode progressively fills the scene from the back toward the camera with virtual water. Distant areas disappear under the virtual water, while only nearby objects remain "dry." The fourth mode, Sonar, skips the display entirely and turns depth into sound. It analyzes how crowded the left and right sides of the camera view are, producing low clicks for the left and higher clicks for the right. The clicks become faster as objects get closer. Walk toward a wall and the clicking accelerates; point the camera toward an open doorway and it slows or stops. Getting all of this running locally on the hardware required some optimization. Depth Anything V2 Small was configured to use a 336×252 input and run in full floating-point precision. According to Alexander's testing, reducing the input resolution provided a better tradeoff than 8-bit quantization, which introduced depth artifacts and flattened the model's near field. The NPU runs an inference in about 16 milliseconds, leaving the VENTUNO Q's eight CPU cores available for capturing video, drawing the interface, and generating audio. Camera capture, inference, and rendering are also split between three threads so the NPU can begin processing the next image while the current result is being displayed. Alexander could push inference to around 30 frames per second, but that increased board power consumption to 15.2 watts. Limiting the application to 20 FPS and using the NPU's balanced power mode drops consumption to 11.8 watts, letting the VENTUNO Q, 10-inch display, and webcam run together from a USB-C power bank. The project doesn't even touch the VENTUNO Q's STM32 microcontroller, leaving it available for future additions such as physical controls, vibration motors, or other hardware tied to the depth data. queue.rss: Soft robots are valued for their ability to safely handle delicate objects, but they usually need separate sensors, actuators, wiring, and control electronics to make that happen. Researchers at KAIST have taken a different approach by creating a single soft material that can detect a nearby object, move to grasp it, and then hold that position for more than 10 minutes after the power is removed. Inspired by the Venus flytrap, the team's " Ionograsper " combines sensing and actuation into a single ionic polymer. Instead of relying on continuous electrical power or complex pneumatic systems, the material responds to a brief pulse of ultraviolet light and then passively maintains its shape, dramatically reducing the energy needed to perform a grasping task. The actuator is built from an ionogel mounted on a flexible PDMS substrate. Its active layer combines a hygroscopic polymer with azobenzene molecules, which change shape when exposed to UV light. Those molecules form an ionically crosslinked network that not only produces mechanical movement but also leaves mobile ions free to respond to electrical changes in the surrounding environment. When UV light strikes the material, the azobenzene molecules rapidly undergo photoisomerization while localized heating drives moisture out of the illuminated surface. Rather than simply bending once and returning to its original position, the material follows a more complex sequence. It first bends toward the light as the exposed surface dehydrates. After the light is removed, nanoscale pores created during irradiation allow moisture from the surrounding air to re-enter the outer surface more quickly than the interior. That uneven rehydration causes the material to bend in the opposite direction, where it remains for more than 10 minutes before gradually relaxing back to its original shape. The material also functions as a proximity sensor. As a charged object approaches, mobile ions redistribute throughout the polymer and form an electric double layer, generating a measurable voltage without requiring an external sensing bias. That allows the soft actuator to detect nearby objects before making contact, providing a built-in feedback mechanism without additional sensing hardware. To demonstrate the concept, the researchers fabricated a biomimetic soft gripper that autonomously detected approaching objects through the generated voltage signal before a brief UV pulse triggered the grasp. Because the deformed shape is mechanically locked after illumination, the gripper continues holding the object without continuous power until the polymer slowly relaxes and releases it. The complete grasping cycle requires only about 35.3 mW/cm² during actuation, significantly reducing energy consumption compared to conventional soft robotic systems that require sustained power. While the technology remains at the research stage, the team believes the approach could simplify future soft robotic systems by replacing separate sensors and actuators with multifunctional materials. Current work is focused on extending sensing range, improving durability and load capacity, increasing actuation speed, and replacing UV activation with visible or near-infrared light for more practical real-world applications.This soft robot can sense and grasp in unconventional ways (📷: Y. queue.rss: The Arduino UNO Q is designed to bring Linux, AI acceleration, and real-time microcontroller control together on a single board, and Robodog V2.0 is a good example of what that combination makes possible. The project upgrades the Yahboom DOGZILLA S2 by installing an UNO Q as its primary computer while leaving the robot's original motion controller in charge of driving the servos. This gives the quadruped computer vision, a browser-based control interface, and onboard sensors without changing the hardware responsible for walking. The project builds around DOGZILLA's existing architecture. The original servo controller remains connected using Yahboom's UART protocol, while the UNO Q takes over as the robot's main computing platform. The board combines a Qualcomm QRB2210 processor running Debian Linux with an STM32U585 Cortex-M33 microcontroller, allowing Linux applications and deterministic real-time control to coexist on the same hardware. The microcontroller runs a RouterBridge-based Arduino sketch that exposes commands including walking, turning, stopping, checking battery status, and other preset actions. Python software running under Linux communicates with the microcontroller, and the microcontroller translates those requests into the UART packets expected by the DOGZILLA controller. That separation lets the existing motion hardware continue doing what it was designed for while the Linux side handles higher-level behavior. Those higher-level features are built with Arduino App Lab. A Python application provides a web interface that includes manual driving controls, preset actions, live USB camera streaming, system status, gamepad support, and more. OpenCV manages the camera feed, while object detection models from Qualcomm AI Hub or Edge Impulse perform inference directly on the robot. Because everything runs locally, the system can recognize objects and gestures without relying on cloud services. In addition, a Modulino LED Matrix serves as an animated face, displaying expressions, arrows, battery indicators, and visual feedback during operation. A Modulino Movement module contributes accelerometer and vibration sensing, and a Modulino Buzzer provides audible status notifications. The software can also configure the UNO Q as its own Wi-Fi access point, allowing a phone or laptop to connect directly to the robot and access the web interface without an external network. That makes the platform self-contained for demonstrations, classrooms, or robotics development. Robodog V2.0 is intended as an educational and prototyping platform, but it also shows what makes the UNO Q different from a typical Linux development board. By combining a full Debian environment with an onboard Arduino-compatible microcontroller, it can run AI models, host a modern web interface, process camera data, and still provide deterministic real-time control. queue.rss: If you need a boost converter for your electronics project, you can pick one up for a few dollars. But if your project draws a couple of hundred amps, these converters aren't going to cut it. YouTuber Nick Electronics wanted to power a 48V trolling motor with a 12V battery, so he had to build a custom boost converter that can deliver up to 200 amps. It uses six interleaved power stages, aluminum-core circuit boards, thick copper bus bars, and a CNC-machined enclosure to handle the kilowatts of power flowing through it. Rather than asking a single boost stage to carry the full 200 amps, the converter divides the load between six phases. Each handles roughly 33 amps, reducing conduction losses while also spreading heat across more components. The phases are packed closely together on the main power board, with wide copper pours and short connections used to keep resistance and parasitic inductance as low as possible. Instead of standard FR4, Nick uses a four-layer insulated-metal substrate board with an aluminum base. Thick copper layers carry the current, while thermally conductive dielectric layers transfer heat into the aluminum substrate. Once installed, the PCB can dump that heat directly into the CNC-machined aluminum enclosure beneath it, which doubles as a large heat sink. That thermal performance made assembling the board quite a lot harder. During the first reflow attempt, a hot plate heated the thin aluminum PCB unevenly and caused it to bow upward. Once the center lifted away from the hot plate, there was no longer enough heat reaching parts of the board to properly melt the solder paste. The solution was a 5 mm thick aluminum backing plate drilled and tapped so the PCB could be bolted completely flat. With the board clamped against the plate, Nick was able to heat the assembly evenly enough to successfully reflow the surface-mount components. The completed board was then preheated to around 150°C while the much larger through-hole parts were soldered into place. Those parts include six hefty inductors mounted vertically to save board space and keep connections short. Custom FR4 supports were milled and bonded to the inductors to keep them stable. Current enters and leaves through 4 mm thick tinned copper bus bars, which were cut, drilled for M8 terminals, tapped, and carefully bent to clear the enclosure. Control electronics live on a separate PCB mounted above the power stage. It contains an STM32 microcontroller and dedicated multiphase PWM controllers, connecting to the lower board through dense pin headers. Keeping this circuitry separate also leaves the high-current power planes relatively uninterrupted and isolates sensitive control electronics from some of the switching noise below. Even the enclosure is part of the electrical and thermal design. Its CNC-machined aluminum pieces were bead-blasted and bonded together with structural epoxy before the power hardware was installed. Coming in at $1,000 in parts, Nick's boost converter isn't cheap, but it can power just about anything you throw at it. Tobi, le créateur de la chaîne éponyme comme on dit, Game of Tobi , a publié une vidéo où Super Mario 64 tourne sur une Super Nintendo, avec la puce Super FX. Alors pour l'instant, seuls quelques niveaux fonctionnent, mais ils fonctionnent sur la VRAIE console !! Et ça c'est grâce à une cartouche flash compatible avec cette puce. Pour la petite histoire si vous n'en avez jamais entendu parler, cette puce SuperFX c'est en réalité un coprocesseur conçu par Argonaut qui équipait déjà Star Fox et Yoshi's Island (Alors ça vous revient les gamers grisonnants ??)

Ce clic autorise une connexion à Google : adresse IP transmise et traceurs possibles. En savoir plus

Hé je vous arrête tout de suite, ce n'est pas le jeu de la Nintendo 64 recompilé, non pour ça faudrait utiliser mon logiciel Kompote . En réalité, Tobi a écrit un moteur maison qui réutilise les assets d'origine, animations comprises. Ce moteur dessine donc l'image depuis l'arrière vers l'avant (ça s'appelle l'algorithme du peintre ) plutôt que de passer par un Z-buffer classique (la mémoire qui retient la profondeur de chaque pixel). Il écarte aussi très agressivement tout ce qu'il peut ne pas dessiner et c'est vrai parfois trop, ce qui fait que ça réduit le niveau de détail des textures. C'est voulu par Tobi car les textures sont un énorme goulot d'étranglement !

Quoiqu'il en soit, Tobi trouve le résultat sympa car juste "reconnaissable" et est surtout content de Bob-omb Battlefield, l'un des niveaux de Mario 64 les plus hardus à faire tourner de façon fluide. En tout cas c'est un sacré challenge pour lui car les niveaux doivent tenir dans 2 Mo max. Il cherche donc comment réduire au max tout ça.

Maintenant, certains d'entre vous se sont peut-être demandé d'où sortait ce nom "Super Mario FX" ?

Eh bien Tobi reprend là une vieille rumeur qui raconte que Nintendo aurait préparé un premier Mario en 3D pour la Super Nintendo avec cette puce SuperFX, avant malheureusement de l'annuler pour en faire le Super Mario 64 qu'on connait tous ! Moi ce que j'ai pu trouver sur cette rumeur, c'est via SNES Central qui a fini par poser la question à Dylan Cuthbert, l'un des programmeurs de Star Fox qui a expliqué que Super Mario FX était en réalité le nom de code interne de la puce FX, et non celui d'un jeu. Bref, à vous de voir si vous préférez les faits à la rumeur plus romanesque ^^.

Maintenant si vous voulez jouer à sa version de Super Mario FX, il faudra patienter car rien n'est téléchargeable pour l'instant. Sniiiif ! En effet, Tobi veut publier le projet de façon à ce que chacun puisse le compiler avec sa propre copie de Super Mario 64, ce qui lui évitera de finir en octogone avec les avocats de Nintendo !

queue.rss: Even with easy access to 3D printers, makers still like to hide electronics inside all sorts of unusual objects. But it's not every day that you see an entire Wi-Fi smart remote stuffed inside a walnut. Yet that's exactly what YouTuber JSK-koubou set out to do, transforming a real walnut shell into a rechargeable ESP32-C3-powered infrared remote that can learn commands from existing remotes, control appliances over Wi-Fi, and even report the room temperature. The project starts with an ordinary walnut carefully split into two halves. JSK-koubou removes the internal ribs with a rotary tool to recover as much space as possible, then installs tiny neodymium magnets around the edges to hold the shell closed. Four holes around the perimeter accommodate the IR LEDs, while another opening provides access to the USB-C connector used for charging and programming. Inside, the remote is built around a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32C3. The tiny board provides both the processing power and Wi-Fi connection while leaving just enough room for a 300 mAh LiPo battery. An IR receiver mounted directly against the XIAO lets the device learn commands from an existing remote, while a push button, status LED, and temperature sensor provide additional input and feedback. Getting enough infrared power out of something this small required a separate driver circuit. Four high-power IR LEDs are switched by a MOSFET, with their power coming directly from the LiPo battery rather than through the XIAO's regulator. A resistor limits current, and GPIO D3 controls the MOSFET. The LEDs are positioned in different directions around the shell, providing broad IR coverage without requiring the walnut to be pointed directly at the device being controlled. Most of the wiring is done with thin enamel-coated magnet wire to conserve space. Where wires cross between the two halves of the walnut, flexible stranded wire is used instead so repeated opening doesn't fatigue the conductors. JSK-koubou also added white diffuser caps over the IR LEDs to make the finished walnut look a little less like it is filled with electronics. The ESP32-C3 connects to the local Wi-Fi network and serves its own browser-based control interface. Users can aim an existing remote at the IR receiver to capture and store its raw timing data, then replay those commands. The onboard temperature sensor can also report room temperature through the interface, making it possible to check conditions and remotely turn on an air conditioner. With the device waking every five minutes, a 24-hour test consumed about 47 mAh, suggesting roughly six days of operation from the 300 mAh battery. If a walnut case isn't your thing, there are other options. JSK-koubou later built a more practical 3D-printed desktop version with an improved LED driver and ventilation around the temperature sensor. queue.rss: Microsoft has officially launched WSL containers, a new feature for its Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) that make it easy to build, run, and deploy Linux containers on Windows — and to provide Windows applications with programmatic access to said containers. "WSL is central to our commitment to making Windows the best place to build, run, and manage Linux workloads," says Logan Iyer, corporate vice-president for the Windows platform and developer at Microsoft, quietly ignoring that one would expect Linux to be the best place to build, run, and manage Linux workloads. "As AI [Artificial Intelligence], cloud-native development, containers, and open-source ecosystems continue to converge on Linux, more developers are choosing to perform these workloads directly on Windows devices. We're continuing our journey towards this goal with a new feature in WSL: WSL containers." WSL containers, Iyer explains, stands in as an alternative to existing container management systems like Docker, allowing Windows Subsystem for Linux — an optional Windows feature that allows an entire Linux operating system to run within Windows, for access to Linux-specific software and tools — to manage containers itself. A command-line interface provides a way to easily build, run, and deploy Linux containers on Windows, while an application programming interface (API) provides a way for native Windows applications to handle containers themselves — allowing a Windows app to deploy a container for task-specific workloads, Iyer explains. "Similarly to WSL, client processes call into 'wslservice.exe', which is a privileged Windows service. That service has the capability to create virtual machines (via HCS), and use those to run Linux workflows," explains Microsoft senior software engineer Pierre Boulay of how the new architecture differs. "A key difference with WSL's architecture though is that wslservice.exe does not retain ownership of the virtual machine. Instead, it creates a child process, wslcsession.exe, which runs on behalf of the calling user and will perform all session operations (creating containers, mounting directories, binding networking ports, etc) on behalf of the user. "This new model allows WSLC to have both strong isolation between sessions, since they live in different processes, but also reinforced security boundaries, since sessions operations are executed in a less privileged process than wslservice.exe." The WSL container feature is now available in all new WSL installations, and can be added to existing installations with wsl --update . More information is available in Boulay's technical overview , with source code available on GitHub under the permissive MIT license. Microsoft has added a new built-in container management system to the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). (📷: Microsoft)
